source: Jacobs (2019) The Mathematics of Changing one's Mind, via Jeffrey's or via Pearl's update rule
finding: Soft evidence can be handled two ways. Jeffrey's rule treats it as a new state of affairs: a convex mix of the point updates. Pearl's virtual evidence treats it as a likelihood, an extra node with strength r. They agree at r=0 and r=1 and differ in between.
numbers: Disease test: prior 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive 5%. Pr(d|pos)=15%, Pr(d|neg)=0.1%. With 80% certainty of a positive reading, Jeffrey gives about 12% (0.8x15%+0.2x0.1%); Pearl gives about 3%.
quote: Jeffrey's rule says we should take the convex combination, with factors 0.8 and 0.2
limits: Paper itself says it cannot tell which rule is 'right'; gives only a vague guide (adjust to a new state vs factor in evidence). No human data.
agent_relevance: Test (S4) must say which kind of noisy check it has. 'I am 80% sure the output was a pass' (Jeffrey) and 'the checker has this hit rate' (Pearl) give different numbers, 12% vs 3% here.

source: Jacobs (2019), same paper: formal properties
finding: Jeffrey updating with the already-predicted state changes nothing. Successive Jeffrey updates in general do not commute. Pearl updates do commute. The two rules coincide on point (hard) evidence. Pearl evidence can be rewritten as Jeffrey evidence.
numbers: Proposition 5.3 (1)-(4); Pearl commutativity is Proposition 4.3(3).
limits: Non-commutativity is read by the author as possibly a feature (order effects like priming), but that is an analogy, not data.
agent_relevance: If the agent logs checks as Jeffrey-style shifts, the order of checks changes the result. Log checks as likelihood ratios (Pearl style) so order does not matter.

source: Munk, Mead, Wood (2023) Uncertain Evidence in Probabilistic Models and Stochastic Simulators
finding: Compares Jeffrey's rule, Pearl's virtual evidence and Tolpin's distributional evidence. Jeffrey's rule needs the conditional p(x|y) to stay fixed. The three give different posteriors for the same stated uncertainty, so the reading of the uncertainty is a modelling choice.
numbers: Three simulated cases: Gaussian toy, ball drop (x=1 m, timing error 0.03 s, observed 0.43 s vs ideal 0.45 s, g=9.81), Kepler-90 orbit (7 transits, 20 min measurement error, 10 min model error). In the ball drop, distributional evidence puts near-zero mass on the true g; in the Kepler case only the orbital period P differs under Jeffrey, while e, omega and omega+M agree.
quote: misinterpretations of uncertain evidence can lead to vastly different inference results
limits: Simulation only, with the 'correct' interpretation set by the authors. Jeffrey's rule can be inconsistent with the base model; then change the model or get better data.
agent_relevance: Before applying a noisy-check update, check that the check's claimed distribution is compatible with the agent's own model. If not, do not apply it blindly.

source: Munk et al. (2023), same paper: Jeffrey as KL-closest update
finding: Jeffrey's rule gives the new joint closest in KL divergence to the old one, subject to the new marginal on y (credited to Peng et al., 2010). Grove and Halpern (1997) treat the same problem as inference over models given trusted statements.
numbers: Not numeric. Virtual evidence posterior is proportional to sum_k lambda_k p(y_k,x) (Eq. 3).
limits: Secondary citation of Peng et al. and Grove-Halpern; those originals were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives the minimal-change justification for letting a noisy check shift but not zero a candidate.

source: Jacobs and Stein (2023) Pearl's and Jeffrey's Update as Modes of Learning in Probabilistic Programming
finding: Pearl's update raises expected validity; Jeffrey's update lowers KL divergence (a variational-inference view). Both agree on one test. On repeated tests they can disagree wildly.
numbers: Prevalence 5%, sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%, results pos,pos,neg. Three WebPPL programs give 64% (prog1, condition on each test), 9% (prog2) and 33% (prog3, nested inference). With 3000 tests (2000 pos, 1000 neg) prog1 goes to about 100%, the others stay put.
limits: Programs differ in how repeated tests are modelled; the paper does not claim one is empirically right.
agent_relevance: Repeated noisy checks of one candidate can be counted as independent (prog1, goes to certainty) or as one average signal (prog2/3). Check errors from one model are correlated (G4), so do not count repeats as independent.

source: Wagner (1992/2013) Generalizing Jeffrey Conditionalization
finding: Conditioning is right only if you judge q(E)=1 and q(A|E)=p(A|E). Jeffrey's rule drops the first demand: q(A)=sum over cells of q(E_i) p(A|E_i). Wagner lets evidence set only a lower bound on the new probability (Dempster lower probability, 2-monotone capacity), with classic Jeffrey as the case of disjoint focal elements.
numbers: No experiments.
quote: Radical probabilism recoils from dogmatic judgments like q(E) = 1
limits: Mathematical paper; the generalisation is about imprecise priors.
agent_relevance: Supports 'the check bounds the shift' rather than fixing it exactly, if the agent is unsure how reliable a check is.

source: Smets (1993) Jeffrey's rule of conditioning generalized to belief functions
finding: Jeffrey needs two things: new weights on a partition (R1) and unchanged ratios inside each cell (R2). Smets gives geometric and Dempster-style versions for belief functions. Bayes' rule is the limiting case where one cell gets probability 1.
numbers: No numbers; formal.
limits: Different generalisations give different answers; no empirical test. Only the opening sections were read closely.
agent_relevance: If the agent keeps hypothesis sets as belief functions, noisy checks have more than one valid update.

source: Yu (2021) Bayesian Neural Networks with Soft Evidence
finding: Two algorithms approximate Jeffrey conditionalization when the labels are soft (annotator distributions). Jeffrey-based nets matched or beat baselines on accuracy and improved calibration.
numbers: Calibration gains 'upwards of 20%' in some cases. CIFAR-10H (10,000 images, soft labels): accuracies about 46-47.5%; the printed table has NLL near 1.9-2.0 for the best methods vs 3.9 for one baseline (row alignment from pdf text is uncertain).
quote: it seems almost wasteful and anti-Bayesian to throw away the uncertainty
limits: Small image models; the soft labels come from human annotators, so the true distribution is unknown. The paper leaves Jeffrey's correctness as a philosophical debate.
agent_relevance: Keeping the uncertainty in a label (not rounding to a hard label) helps calibration. Same idea as keeping a noisy check as a shift.

source: Zhao and Osherson (2010) Updating beliefs in light of uncertain evidence: Descriptive assessment of Jeffrey's rule
finding: Tests whether people keep the relevant conditional probabilities fixed (invariance) when evidence is uncertain. Experiment 1 used Jeffrey's candlelight example; Experiment 2 used one scenario where invariance seems fair and one where it does not. Results roughly fit Jeffrey's principle.
numbers: Per-study N and effect sizes not read (only the abstract was seen on a Princeton record page).
limits: Abstract only. The claim 'roughly conformed' needs the full paper.
agent_relevance: Humans roughly respect the rigidity condition, but it can fail when the scenario makes the conditional suspect. The agent must test that within-cell beliefs really stay fixed.

source: Hadjichristidis, Sloman and Over (2014) Categorical induction from uncertain premises: Jeffrey's doesn't completely rule
finding: Three studies on induction from uncertain premises such as 'there is an 80% chance falcons have an ulnar artery'. They compare Jeffrey's rule with the rule of total probability. The title says Jeffrey's rule does not fully describe judgments.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Known only from a search-result summary; no figures verified.
agent_relevance: Even humans do not follow Jeffrey exactly. Treat it as a norm to check against, not a description of behaviour.

source: Over and Hadjichristidis (2009) Uncertain premises and Jeffrey's rule (BBS commentary)
finding: Commentary arguing that Jeffrey's rule is not constrained enough to account for actual probability judgments from uncertain premises.
numbers: None read.
limits: Seen only as a search snippet; the page returned 503.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'Jeffrey' alone predicts nothing unless the invariance conditions are fixed.

source: Jeffrey (1965) The Logic of Decision; Jeffrey (1983/1990) probability kinematics
finding: Rule: P_new(A) = sum_i P(A|E_i) P_new(E_i) over a partition E_i. Founding example: seeing a cloth by candlelight, unsure if it is green, blue or violet. Condition: the P(A|E_i) do not change (rigidity). Ordinary conditioning is the case P_new(E_j)=1.
numbers: Not numeric.
limits: From background knowledge, not opened this session. Confirmed in outline by Jacobs, Munk and Wagner, which were read.
agent_relevance: Defines the S4 update: shift the weights on cells, keep within-cell beliefs.

source: Diaconis and Zabell (1982) Updating subjective probability, JASA
finding: Classic analysis of Jeffrey updating: when it is justified, how it relates to minimal-distance updates, and that successive Jeffrey updates are order dependent.
numbers: Not read; secondary reports (Jacobs, Munk) agree on non-commutativity.
limits: From background knowledge and secondary mentions; exact theorems not verified.
agent_relevance: Expect order effects when several noisy checks are applied in turn.

source: Chan and Darwiche (2005) On the revision of probabilistic beliefs using uncertain evidence; Pearl (1988)
finding: Jeffrey and Pearl are two ways of specifying a shift: Jeffrey states the posterior wanted, Pearl states the evidence strength (a Bayes factor). One can be converted into the other.
numbers: Not read.
quote: The difference between Jeffrey's rule and Pearl's method is in the way uncertain evidence is specified
limits: The quoted sentence comes from Jacobs (2019), which was read; the conversion result is background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Store each noisy check as a Bayes factor. It is prior-independent and order-safe, and can be turned into a Jeffrey shift for any prior.

source: Dietrich, List and Bradley (2016) Belief revision generalized: a joint characterization of Bayes's and Jeffrey's rules
finding: Cited in Jacobs (2019, Example 6.4) as an example where both Jeffrey-style and Pearl-style updates are used, for different reasons.
numbers: None.
limits: Only seen through Jacobs' citation.
agent_relevance: The choice of rule depends on what the evidence is.

source: Filbry, Melo and Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Without reasoning, LLMs break Bayes' rule when updating on evidence in context. With reasoning and code, updates become close to the oracle. Models rebuild likelihoods and Bayes' rule correctly; errors are numerical slips.
numbers: Models include Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen. Non-reasoning LLM updates cut final success by at least 30% versus the oracle across all models, near 0% for weaker models on 20 Questions. With reasoning, Gemma-4-31B-it matches the oracle on ProteinWorld-simple; a Gemini-2.5-Pro reasoning-only trace put 85% mass on a hypothesis whose true posterior was 0.261.
limits: Evidence is noise-free outcomes, not Jeffrey-style soft evidence. Preprint, Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model compute the update in its head. Have code do the update from stated likelihood ratios.

source: Filbry et al. (2026), coherence section
finding: Probabilities elicited in separate chats are often Dutch-bookable; inside one dialogue they are mostly coherent.
numbers: Across conversations, violation rates exceed 50% of 30 scenarios for almost all model-constraint combinations. Within one dialogue they fall to 10% for Gemini and to one scenario of 30 for Gemma.
limits: 30 forecasting scenarios, three violation types; the paper says this does not show universal coherence.
agent_relevance: Keep the whole belief table in one context and let code, not repeated fresh prompts, compute each shift.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench: Evaluating LLM Belief Trajectories Under Multi-Turn Evidence Accumulation
finding: Seven LLMs (3B to 70B) track a coin's bias over turns. Scaling improves latent inference but not downstream prediction. Larger models over-react, giving more extreme probabilities than the Bayesian reference. The third task filters observations through a persona (a noisy channel).
numbers: Seven models: LLaMA 3B/8B/70B and Qwen 3B/7B/14B/32B. Design follows the bookbag-and-poker-chip paradigm (Phillips and Edwards 1966). Effect sizes beyond 'overshoot or undershoot' were not extracted.
limits: Preprint; details of the persona channel beyond the abstract were not read in full.
agent_relevance: Opposite of the human pattern (conservatism). A noisy check could push a model to near zero or near one, so the S4 rule must cap the shift.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs in a five-round flight-recommendation task improve little after round one and fall well short of a Bayesian assistant. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's predictions fixes much of it and transfers to hotels and web shopping.
numbers: 624 simulated users; Gemma 2 9B/27B, Llama 3 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B. Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time, more than original or oracle-tuned. Human subset: 48 users; humans also fall short.
limits: Evidence is the user's choices (noise-free); needs training, so not usable in a no-training scaffold.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting does not give Bayesian updating; supports having the program, not the model, hold the posterior.

source: Gupta et al. (2025) Enough Coin Flips Can Make LLMs Act Bayesian
finding: With in-context coin flips, LLMs often start with biased priors, then follow Bayesian posterior updates. Deviations come mostly from miscalibrated priors, not wrong updates. In-context evidence outweighs explicit instructions about the bias.
numbers: Zero-shot models ascribe roughly 60-80% probability of heads to a coin; a Llama3.1-8B example is plotted against a posterior mean of 0.88.
limits: Binary, noise-free evidence, single parameter.
agent_relevance: Priors from the model are a weak point. Set the prior in code from base rates.

source: Nafar, Venable and Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over Uncertain Text by Generative LLMs (BLInD)
finding: BLInD tests probabilistic reasoning over text with explicit probabilities. Accuracy falls as variables rise; mapping the text to code or a probabilistic program holds up better.
numbers: Accuracy 100% at 2 variables falling to as low as 73% at 9 variables for the weaker setups; GPT-3.5 above 90% overall with the best mapping; test set of 900 instances.
limits: Explicit probabilities in Bayesian networks; not a test of uncertain-evidence updates as such.
agent_relevance: Extract the numbers, then compute outside the model.

source: Schrader et al. (2024) QUITE: Quantifying Uncertainty in Natural Language Text in Bayesian Reasoning Scenarios
finding: Benchmark of Bayesian reasoning with verbal probabilities (words like 'unlikely', 'almost certain') and evidence statements. Neuro-symbolic approaches do much better than direct prompting.
numbers: Exact accuracies not extracted this session (figure only).
limits: Partial read; numbers missing.
agent_relevance: Verbal hedges in a check ('probably passed') need a fixed word-to-number table in code.

source: Phillips and Edwards (1966) Conservatism in a simple probability inference task; Edwards (1968/1982)
finding: Classic bookbag-and-poker-chip result: people update toward the Bayesian answer but not far enough (conservatism). Named in BayesBench as the paradigm adapted.
numbers: Not read; no figures.
limits: Background knowledge and BayesBench's mention. Exact multipliers not verified.
agent_relevance: Human default is under-update; LLM default (BayesBench) is over-update. Set the S4 rule against the LLM bias.

source: Field (1978) A note on Jeffrey conditionalization; Skyrms (1987) Dynamic coherence and probability kinematics
finding: Field restated Jeffrey input as a Bayes factor to fix order dependence. Skyrms gave a diachronic Dutch-book argument for Jeffrey conditioning under rigidity.
numbers: None.
limits: Background knowledge only, not opened.
agent_relevance: The Bayes-factor form is order-safe.

source: Pearl (1990) Jeffrey's rule, passage of experience, and neo-Bayesianism
finding: Argues that uncertain observations should be read as likelihoods (virtual evidence), specified by the reliability of the source rather than by the final posterior.
numbers: None.
limits: From memory of title and thesis; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports specifying checks by their reliability, not by the resulting belief.
